forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Eastbourne repays government bailout as debt repayment generates £12.9m saving
news_drafts.lead: Eastbourne Borough Council has repaid Exceptional Financial Support, the government bailout funding it received earlier, after delivering a financial recovery plan centred on debt reduction. In October 2025, the council used asset sale proceeds to repay £25m of long-term loans from the Public Works Loan Board (PWLB, the government's lending arm for councils), generating a discount saving of £12.9m that will reduce financing costs by £1.49m over the year. This accelerated debt repayment has materially improved the council's finances: the proportion of General Fund spending consumed by debt service fell from 43.8% in 2024/25 to 25.2%, freeing capacity for other investment. Total external debt fell to £150.7m. The council's housing stock (Housing Revenue Account) saw financing costs rise to 31.1% of rental income, a 3.4 percentage point increase attributed to higher depreciation charges rather than rising interest. Capital spending underspent budget by 27%, at £31.9m against £44m budgeted, with borrowing requirement falling to £7.4m from a £25m budget.

news_drafts.headline: Eastbourne's housing investment stalls as regulatory costs mount without government funding
news_drafts.lead: Eastbourne Borough Council's £28.4m housing new build programme is forecast to spend only £16.8m this year, leaving £11.7m unspent. The shortfall stems from multiple project delays: the Bedwardwell Road scheme has been re-tendered following contractor issues; two schemes funded by the government's Social and Affordable Housing Programme have experienced grant delays; and three acquisition properties are not expected to complete until the third quarter. Meanwhile, the council faces mounting financial pressure from new housing regulations. The government has not provided funding for changes required of social landlords, the council notes, even as two major regulatory regimes take effect within ten weeks: Awaab's Law Phase 2, extending mandatory hazard inspections and remedies beyond damp and mould, and the Conduct and Competence Standard, requiring staff qualifications and workforce policy overhaul. These pressures will need to be considered within the council's 30-year housing business plan.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Annual Report of Audit and Governance Committee 2025-26
findings.headline: Statement of Accounts for 2024-25 signed on time after council was previously behind on statutory compliance
findings.detail: The Committee provided proactive support to ensure timely signing of the 2024-25 Statement of Accounts with External Auditors' Value for Money commentary, thereby bringing the council up to date with central Government's back stop arrangements. The phrase "up to date" indicates the council had previously not been in compliance with statutory deadlines.
findings.matters: Timely signed accounts with unqualified audit opinions are essential for financial credibility. The council catching up from prior non-compliance to current compliance demonstrates resolution of an administrative governance problem.
findings.quote: Proactive support to help ensure the Council was in position to sign the Statement of Accounts for 2024-25, which included the External Auditors commentary on the Council's Value for Money, thus bringing the Council up to date with central Government's back stop arrangements.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Annual Report of Audit and Governance Committee 2025-26
findings.headline: Audit Committee governance framework has gaps against CIPFA guidance
findings.detail: The self-assessment identified that the Committee's Terms of Reference lack explicit reference to value for money and internal audit independence oversight. The Committee has not held private meetings with auditors (planning to start in 2026-27). No formal evaluation of member skills and training needs occurred in the past two years. These gaps were identified as areas where alignment with CIPFA guidance would strengthen the governance framework.
findings.matters: Governance framework gaps in the audit committee suggest the council's oversight assurance function itself may have blind spots. A weak audit committee means weaker oversight of management performance and financial controls.
findings.quote: the review has identified this as an area where greater clarity and alignment would strengthen the governance framework.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Annual Report of Audit and Governance Committee 2025-26
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation poses potential governance and control challenges
findings.detail: The Committee recognises potential governance, risk and control challenges if a new unitary authority for East Sussex proceeds. This is identified as a key focus area for 2026-27 and beyond. The Committee has already requested briefings on HR resource planning implications, indicating significant organisational change is being considered.
findings.matters: LGR represents major organisational change creating operational risk and governance uncertainty. A lender needs to understand how financial controls and management systems will function during significant restructuring.
findings.quote: The Committee recognises the potential governance, risk and control challenges arising from Local Government Reorganisation, in addition to existing "business as usual" pressures. Should a new unitary authority for East Sussex be progressed, this will remain a key area of focus during 2026 to 2027 and beyond.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Annual Report of Audit and Governance Committee 2025-26
findings.headline: External auditor's Value for Money findings from 2024-25 deferred for detailed consideration to 2026-27
findings.detail: The Committee states it will undertake further consideration of VFM audit findings during 2026-27, indicating these findings have not yet been fully reviewed or acted upon by the council. This deferral means external audit concerns about efficiency and resource use have not yet been addressed.
findings.matters: Value for Money findings represent external auditor concerns about whether the council is using resources effectively. Delaying review of these findings delays identifying and addressing whatever issues the auditor identified.
findings.quote: The Committee will undertake further consideration of the substantive findings and recommendations arising from the External Auditor's Value for Money work for 2024 to 2025

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Annual Report of Audit and Governance Committee 2025-26
findings.headline: External auditors identified absence of formal escalation process for overdue internal audit recommendations
findings.detail: Grant Thornton noted that there is no formal process requiring departments to explain and provide revised timelines for audit recommendations that are overdue. The Committee plans to implement a formal escalation process in 2026-27. The Committee previously had to petition Corporate Management Team to encourage managers to address outstanding recommendations, indicating this has been a persistent issue.
findings.matters: Absence of formal escalation for audit recommendations indicates a control environment weakness. Without documented accountability procedures, council management can defer addressing audit findings.
findings.quote: there is no formal escalation process for departments to provide written explanations and revised timelines for overdue internal audit recommendations
